summary:
Charal is an interactive wildfire observatory that connects 25 years of NASA satellite fire observations across California. Developed for the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots Harmonization challenge, it combines a monthly fire calendar, animated maps showing how detected fire activity evolves over time, historical comparisons, and downloadable evidence.

MODIS and VIIRS detect fire differently, so combining their raw counts can make a change in satellite technology look like a change in wildfire activity. Charal addresses this through regional machine learning and statistical calibration, explicit uncertainty, and visible data gaps. Its seasonal outlier detection highlights activity in unusual locations or with unusually high intensity relative to local historical patterns, helping users investigate potentially significant events. It also uses independent CAL FIRE perimeter records to investigate the distribution of large wildfire sizes.

By making both patterns and measurement limitations accessible, Charal helps researchers, land managers, and the public interpret long-term fire observations more responsibly. Its California proof of concept provides a transparent foundation for extending the approach to other regions.
details:
Charal is an interactive wildfire observatory that connects 25 years of California satellite observations, from 2001 to 2025. I built it to address a central challenge in studying long-term fire activity: a change in satellite instruments can look like a change in the environment. MODIS and VIIRS detect thermal activity at different resolutions and sensitivities, so simply combining their hotspot counts can create misleading trends.

The project brings more than 1.16 million quality-filtered NASA detections into a linked monthly calendar and interactive map. Users can explore a region, compare seasons and years, animate daily observations, and investigate activity that is unusual for its location and time of year. Separate CAL FIRE perimeter records provide context for documented wildfire events and allow users to examine the distribution of reported fire sizes. Downloadable data, charts, and provenance make the findings easier to inspect and reuse.

To connect the satellite records, I aggregate observations onto a shared monthly grid and estimate earlier MODIS activity on a VIIRS-reference reporting scale. I compare seasonal calibration with machine-learning approaches and evaluate performance across time and geography. The current approach combines seasonal calibration in northern California with a learned count model in southern California, where historical transfer checks support its use. I preserve observed VIIRS reports once available and explicitly mark known incomplete months. This creates a more comparable historical record while keeping the limits of calibration visible.

Charal’s creativity lies in connecting visual storytelling with scientific testing. The calendar makes decades of observations approachable, while the map reveals their spatial and daily patterns. Users can move from an unusual month to the underlying detections and supporting evidence. I also test whether large documented wildfire areas follow a power law, comparing alternative distributions instead of assuming that an appealing pattern must be correct. In the analyzed sample, a simple power law was rejected, and a conditional lognormal fit better.

I developed the application using TypeScript, Nuxt, Vue, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and SVG visualizations. The backend and reproducible analysis pipeline use Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn and Shapely. I also evaluated exploratory neural models.

Throughout development, I considered sensor differences, missing observations, seasonal variation, geographic transfer, uncertainty, accessibility, and reproducibility. I distinguish thermal detections from individual fires and burned area, and I report model limitations and unfavorable results alongside improvements. Later model experiments use previously inspected historical benchmarks, so their gains require independent confirmation.

My intended impact is to help researchers, land managers, educators, and the public ask better questions about changing fire activity. I chose California as a regional proof of concept for a broader approach: make satellite records easier to explore, make comparisons more defensible, and keep the evidence behind each conclusion accessible.

Github project: https://github.com/JonathanDeul/charal
